Project 1

Cybersecurity Lab Series — Network, Web & Binary Security

Python · Bash · Nmap · Burp Suite · Radare2 · Shodan

Self-Directed Cybersecurity Lab Project — 2025

Flags/secrets recovered during these exercises have been redacted from this write-up for responsible disclosure, as they relate to a private lab environment. The descriptions below focus on the tools, techniques and reasoning used rather than the specific answers.

A four-part hands-on lab series I designed and worked through independently, covering the core disciplines of offensive and defensive cybersecurity: network reconnaissance and evasion, web application exploitation, binary reverse engineering, and digital forensics — carried out against a dedicated Kali Linux / Hacklab VM environment.

Network Reconnaissance Web App Exploitation Binary Reverse Engineering Digital Forensics OSINT
4Practical assessment parts completed
10+Distinct security techniques applied
10+Custom Python & Bash scripts written
  • Network reconnaissance & evasion: used Nmap's decoy scanning option alongside Wireshark packet capture to analyse IDS/firewall evasion techniques, and scripted an automated port-knocking sequence (Bash + hping3) to trigger and probe a dynamically opened firewall rule.
  • Web application exploitation: used Burp Suite (Proxy, Repeater) to intercept and manipulate HTTP requests, exploiting a SQL injection vulnerability via a crafted UNION SELECT payload and bypassing a cookie-based authorisation check to escalate privileges on a PHP application.
  • Binary reverse engineering: analysed x86 ELF binaries with Radare2 and Cutter to identify SETUID and stack-overflow vulnerabilities, recovered a ROT13-obfuscated password by writing a custom decoder, and used runtime memory patching in a debugger to bypass an input-size constraint without modifying the binary.
  • Digital forensics & scripting: automated evidence recovery using regex-based log parsing (grep), SHA-256 file identification across large datasets, Python decoders for positional and Base64-encoded secrets, and a multithreaded DNS subdomain brute-force script against a live test domain.
  • Python automation of repetitive forensic tasks: wrote a range of small, single-purpose Python tools to replace manual inspection — recursive filesystem walkers (os.walk, os.path.getsize) that locate a target file by SHA-256 hash or by an exact byte size across nested directories, a frequency counter built with collections.Counter, a leetspeak password-list generator paired with hash verification, and a printable-string extractor that reimplements the strings utility. Each was written to be repeatable and reusable on similar inputs rather than run once by hand.
  • Reproducible tooling and debugging: isolated analysis work in a Python virtual environment (venv) with pinned libraries such as pyelftools to keep the base system clean, and worked methodically through failures — inspecting packet captures, verifying service and firewall state, and correcting debugger argument handling — documenting what was tried even where a given challenge was not solved.
  • OSINT & vulnerability triage: used Shodan to research internet-facing infrastructure for a target organisation and cross-referenced identified service versions against CVSS 2.0 scoring on nvd.nist.gov to assess real-world exploitability.

Project 2

Enterprise Information Security Plan for NZX Limited — ISO/IEC 27005-Aligned Program Incorporating NIST CSF 2.0

ISO/IEC 27001 · 27002 · 27005 · NIST CSF 2.0

ITPG8.770 Cybersecurity in the Enterprise, Master of Information Technology, Eastern Institute of Technology — 2026

Research-based plan developed entirely from publicly available sources (FMA reviews, NZX annual reporting, standards and academic literature). NZX staff were not contacted; details that would only be known to an insider are stated as assumptions in the report.

An enterprise information security program for NZX Limited, operator of New Zealand’s securities, derivatives and clearing markets, designed against the 2025–2026 threat landscape. Using the August 2020 DDoS-driven trading disruption and the Financial Markets Authority’s 2021 and 2026 market-operator reviews as context, the plan sets out security governance roles, a maturity-based training program, an AS/NZS ISO/IEC 27005:2024 risk assessment with controls mapped to ISO/IEC 27002:2022, a NIST CSF 2.0 incident response and continuity model, and two issue-specific security policies.

Information Security Risk Assessment Security Governance Control Mapping Incident Response & BCP Third-Party Risk Security Policy Writing
7Security governance roles defined (3 FMA-mandated)
6Risks rated in the risk register (2 Critical)
19ISO/IEC 27002:2022 controls mapped to risks
2Issue-specific security policies authored
  • Business and regulatory context: analysed NZX’s market operations, licensing under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, its combined operator/frontline-regulator role, and its reliance on a small number of key suppliers (e.g. Spark, Akamai). The FMA’s 2026 review flagged this reliance, together with a lean technology function, as a structural risk.
  • Governance and people: designed a seven-role security governance and reporting structure (CRO, Head of IT Security, Head of Network Architecture, SOC Analyst, IAM Administrator, Incident Response Coordinator, Market Disclosure & Communications Officer) aligned to the NIST NICE Workforce Framework and SFIA 9. It is supported by a role-based training program built on the SANS Security Awareness & Culture Maturity Model and measured by phishing click-through rate, training completion and time-to-report.
  • Risk assessment: applied the AS/NZS ISO/IEC 27005:2024 process to NZX’s critical asset chain (trading → matching engine → market data → clearing → settlement → disclosure). Six technical, operational and human-factor risks were rated on a likelihood/impact matrix and heat map, with DDoS and extortion-driven disruption rated Critical. An Annualised Loss Expectancy example was used to support the qualitative ratings.
  • Mitigation and controls: mapped treatments to ISO/IEC 27002:2022 controls: DDoS scrubbing and network-path redundancy, independent failover for the Market Announcement Platform, ICT continuity planning, contractual vendor assurance, encryption, MDR/SIEM monitoring, call-back verification against AI-enabled executive impersonation, and tiered vulnerability and penetration testing (OWASP/PTES) with 30-day remediation of critical findings. The plan is strictly defensive and justifies ruling out hack-back on legal and ethical grounds.
  • Strategic options and residual risk: compared internal, outsourced and hybrid security operating models and recommended the hybrid model, which keeps governance in-house and outsources 24/7 SOC monitoring and scrubbing. After treatment, residual risk for DDoS and third-party dependency was assessed as Medium.
  • Incident response and continuity: structured incident response on the NIST CSF 2.0 community profile (SP 800-61r3) with a SANS practitioner playbook, set RTO/RPO targets by system priority supported by a Business Impact Analysis (SP 800-184), and built in Privacy Act 2020 breach-notification and continuous-disclosure obligations. Program KPIs/KRIs (MTTD/MTTR, critical vulnerabilities closed within SLA, RTO/RPO test success) are reported quarterly to the CRO and Board Technology Committee.
  • Security policies: wrote two ISSPs adapted from SANS templates using the Whitman & Mattord ISSP structure. The first is a Password Protection Policy aligned to NIST SP 800-63B-4: 14-character minimum, MFA for privileged and remote access, and password changes triggered by risk rather than on a fixed schedule. The second is a Market Disclosure & Crisis Communications Policy requiring an accurate initial announcement within one hour and prohibiting minimising language when the root cause is known.

Project 3

Hybrid Cloud Strategy for Critical Infrastructure Resilience — Vector Limited AWS Case Study

AWS Outposts · AWS Transform · Hybrid Cloud · Well-Architected Framework

ITPG8.550 Cloud Based IT Solutions, Master of Information Technology, Eastern Institute of Technology — 2026

An IT consulting analysis of Vector Limited's (New Zealand's largest electricity distributor) hybrid cloud modernisation strategy, evaluating the use of AWS Outposts for latency-critical grid operations and AWS Transform for VMware enterprise workload migration. Applying AWS Academy Cloud Foundations concepts — deployment models, architecture best practices, and scaling & monitoring — the report identifies four core problems, benchmarks strategic alternatives, and proposes governance and monitoring measures for a regulated critical-infrastructure environment.

Hybrid Cloud Architecture Feasibility Analysis SWOT Analysis Zero Trust Security Cloud Migration Strategy
<5msADMS latency achieved via AWS Outposts
35%Five-year TCO reduction vs. on-premises VMware
4Core interconnected problems analysed
9-monthPhased implementation & monitoring plan
  • Problem analysis: identified four interconnected challenges — latency-critical ADMS operations, VMware technical debt and licensing costs, IT/OT convergence cyber-security exposure, and AI-assisted migration governance risk.
  • Feasibility analysis: assessed the strategy across economic, operational and technical dimensions, evaluating dual-rack AWS Outposts active-active resilience against sub-5ms ADMS latency requirements and Direct Connect deterministic connectivity.
  • SWOT & strategic alternatives: benchmarked a full public-cloud migration and an on-premises VMware retention option against the recommended hybrid approach, using the AWS Academy Module 3 deployment-model framework to justify the chosen strategy.
  • Governance recommendations: proposed a zero-trust security architecture (least-privilege access, MFA, IT/OT segmentation), quarterly AWS Well-Architected Reviews across all six pillars, and mandatory human validation gates for AI-assisted migration outputs.
  • Monitoring framework: defined KPIs (uptime, latency, migration success rate, rollback time, security incidents) tracked via CloudWatch dashboards, supported by a phased nine-month implementation roadmap with staged foundation, governance, migration and optimisation phases.

Project 4

Smart Home Automation App for Older Adults — Usability Evaluation

Figma · Maze · Usability Testing

ITPG8.600 Advanced Mobile & Wireless Technologies, Master of IT, Eastern Institute of Technology — 2026

Team project (Sprints 1–5: research, personas, wireframes and prototype design). This case study focuses on my individually authored Sprint 6 deliverable: the usability test plan, evaluation and critical report.

Evaluated a mobile app prototype designed to help independent senior adults (aged 66–86) manage lighting, temperature, security and emergency alerts at home, for a retirement village context. I planned and ran a remote usability test using Maze, analysed the results against the design decisions from earlier sprints, and produced a critical comparison against voice-only assistants and AI-based smart home systems.

View interactive Figma prototype →
Usability Test Design Accessibility Evaluation Comparative Analysis Technical Report Writing Test Planning & Metrics Requirements Traceability IoT & Wireless Protocols AI & Automation Evaluation
100%Task success rate (3 core tasks)
0%Drop-off & misclick rate
99–100Maze usability score
5Participants, aged 66–86
15/20User stories met by final prototype
  • Planned and facilitated an unmoderated remote usability test in Maze covering three core task flows: switch on the light, increase room temperature, and send an SOS alert to a caregiver. Participants were recruited to match the Sprint 3 personas, with a range of technical confidence and minor mobility limitations.
  • Defined the test plan and metrics framework: set test objectives (can users finish core tasks without help; how well the app supports daily control and emergency response) and paired Maze’s automatically recorded metrics (task success, completion time, drop-off, misclicks, full-path and heatmap data) with qualitative indicators such as ease of use and hesitation during navigation.
  • Analysed results and acted on the slowest task: all three tasks reached 100% success with 0% drop-off and 0% misclicks. Temperature (2.8 s) and SOS (4.1 s) were quick, but light control took 11.6 s, so I recommended making the light control more prominent on the dashboard. I also noted that a small sample calls for wider testing.
  • Traced the prototype back to requirements: scored design choices, information architecture and visual accessibility on a 1–5 inspection rubric and checked the prototype against the Sprint 2 technical specification and the 20 Sprint 4 user stories. I found 15 met and 5 not met (including automatic night lighting, automatic heating adjustment and device management), and flagged missing error-recovery features and advanced settings.
  • Team system architecture (Sprint 2): the team specified how the app reaches physical devices. The smartphone connects over Wi-Fi to a SmartThings hub or Raspberry Pi 5 edge gateway, which translates commands into Zigbee, Z-Wave, Bluetooth LE and Matter, with AWS IoT Core and Firebase as the cloud back end. The design also included a tiered voice-confidence fallback (execute above 90%, ask to confirm at 70–89%, switch to touch controls below 70%) so a command never fails silently.
  • Benchmarked the solution against voice-only assistants (Alexa, Google Assistant, Siri) and AI-based automation systems. Voice-only assistants struggle with recognition errors and background noise, while AI automation reduces visibility and user control. I concluded that a hybrid of a visual app, voice input and AI assistance best meets senior users’ need for trust and caregiver support.
  • Evaluated AI and emerging technology (integrated IoT sensors, wearables, AI anomaly detection, 5G/6G) for aged care, and recommended keeping manual controls as a backup when automated systems fail, building data protection in from the start, and training both residents and caregivers.
  • Ran a team retrospective on the four-person team’s delivery across Sprints 1–5. It identified time management and review cycles as the main weaknesses and recommended early internal deadlines, a shared progress tracker (e.g. Planner or Trello) and short regular stand-ups.

Project 5

Last-Mile Delivery Performance Analytics — From Data Wrangling to a Decision-Support Dashboard

Excel · Power Query · Inferential Statistics · Regression · Dashboards

PGQM8.400 Quantitative Methods & Contemporary Tools, Master of Information Technology, Eastern Institute of Technology — 2026 (Assessments 1 & 2)

This case study combines two assessments: Assessment 1 (Parts 1–3: problem scoping, data wrangling, exploratory analysis and statistical inference) and Assessment 2 (Parts 4–5: multivariate modelling and advanced data visualisation). SMP is a fictional New Zealand delivery company. Because no NZ last-mile dataset is publicly available, a public international proxy dataset was used.

An end-to-end quantitative investigation of the question “What operational and environmental factors have a strong impact on delivery time, and how can this improve delivery performance and customer satisfaction?” Using the 43,743-record Amazon Delivery Dataset (Kaggle) as a proxy for SMP’s operations, I cleaned the data in a reproducible Power Query pipeline, identified traffic as the dominant driver through EDA, confirmed it with hypothesis testing and multivariate models, and turned the model into an Excel dashboard and job-level prediction tool for dispatch coordinators.

View source dataset on Kaggle →
Data Wrangling (Power Query) Exploratory Data Analysis Hypothesis Testing Multiple & Logistic Regression Time-Series Analysis Dashboard & Decision-Support Design
43,648Clean records retained (99.8% of raw)
+46 minJam vs. Low traffic delivery gap (d = 0.96)
R² .381Multiple regression fit vs. η² .133 for one-way ANOVA
AUC .919Logistic model predicting late (>150 min) deliveries
  • Problem scoping and dataset evaluation: framed a business problem for a NZ last-mile operator, justified a quantitative approach from the logistics literature, and evaluated the proxy dataset’s suitability and limits (Indian infrastructure, a three-month window, no promised-delivery field).
  • Data wrangling: built a linear, auditable Power Query pipeline that resolved six data-quality issues: export-artefact rows, 91 batch-error records (treated as MNAR and removed listwise), trailing-whitespace duplicate categories, 54 invalid agent ratings (median-imputed and flagged), and 3,495 invalid (0,0) store coordinates (flagged rather than deleted). It also derived Order_Hour, Prep_Time_Min and Distance_km, and 156 impossible-distance outliers were later removed before modelling.
  • Exploratory analysis: used grouped descriptive statistics and eight chart types to show that traffic produced the largest effect (a 46-minute Low-to-Jam gap, compared with 34.6 minutes for weather and 14.7 minutes for vehicle type), along with an evening peak from 19:00 to 21:00 and a Semi-Urban anomaly (n = 152) that was flagged for verification instead of being acted on.
  • Statistical inference: applied a 95% confidence interval, Pearson correlations and a chi-square test, which showed that 96.9% of peak-hour orders fall in Jam traffic (χ² = 39,956.71, Cramér’s V = .96). One-way ANOVA (F(3, 43644) = 2224.86, p < .001) was cross-checked with Welch’s ANOVA after Levene’s test showed unequal variances, followed by Tukey HSD and a one-tailed Welch’s t-test confirming that Jam is significantly slower than Low. The Semi-Urban effect was tested with Welch’s t and Mann-Whitney U.
  • Multivariate modelling: fitted a multiple regression model and used VIF diagnostics to remove the collinear Peak_Hour term (Traffic Jam VIF fell from 12.61 to 1.45). With other factors controlled, the model resolved the EDA’s “motorcycle anomaly” (scooters and vans are about 13.5–14.3 minutes faster) and identified agent rating as a strong lever (−39.1 minutes per rating point).
  • Robustness checks: a logistic regression for SLA breach achieved 86.1% accuracy (pseudo R² = .460), but I noted that its 68.3% sensitivity makes it unsuitable as an SLA-alert tool without recalibration. Time-series analysis found no linear trend, and I diagnosed a near-perfect daily oscillation (lag-1 autocorrelation −0.989) as an artefact of the source data rather than a real operational cycle.
  • Data product: designed the SMP Delivery Performance Dashboard & Prediction Tool in Excel. It includes a KPI band, PivotTable charts with colour-coded slicers, an Order ID lookup (INDEX/MATCH) with an On Time/Delayed status, and a prediction calculator driven by the published regression coefficients (VLOOKUP) with an SLA flag, plus a user manual and a sheet-by-sheet traceability index linking every reported statistic to its source.
  • Critical evaluation: set out the tool’s limitations (61.9% of variance unexplained, no prediction interval, coefficients that cannot be transferred to NZ without revalidation) and recommended a four-week trial of traffic-aware dispatch outside the 19:00–21:00 window before any operational change.

Project 6

NYC Airbnb Market Data Analysis

Python · Pandas · NumPy · Matplotlib

Academic Project — Graduate Certificate in Cyber Security, University of Adelaide, 2025

Analysed a public dataset of 48,895 Airbnb listings across New York City to uncover pricing patterns and their relationship with guest engagement (number of reviews), using Python's data science stack end-to-end — from raw CSV to cleaned dataset to visual insight.

Data Cleaning Descriptive Statistics Groupby Aggregation Data Visualisation NumPy Vectorisation Reusable Functions
  • Cleaned a 48,895-row, 16-column dataset in Pandas by first auditing missing values with df.isnull().sum(), then dropping affected rows and columns (e.g. last_review, reviews_per_month) to produce a tidy frame for analysis.
  • Computed summary statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, quartiles) for rental price (mean $152.72, median $106) and number of reviews, and assembled them into a labelled Pandas DataFrame for clear, readable output.
  • Aggregated with groupby: calculated average rental price per neighbourhood and combined mean price with mean reviews per neighbourhood (groupby().agg()) to drive a neighbourhood-level comparison.
  • Visualised price distribution, price vs. review-count relationships, and pricing variation across NYC neighbourhoods with Matplotlib (histogram, scatter and bar charts).
  • Built a small interactive NumPy tool in the same project: it takes array dimensions as user input, generates a random 2-D array, then reshapes, slices, and splits it into equal parts with validation, and computes mean, median, standard deviation and an element-wise sum across the split — demonstrating vectorised computation and input handling.
  • Wrote reusable Python logic from first principles, including a dictionary-based aggregation routine that computes per-key averages across a list of records using loops and conditionals rather than library shortcuts.

Project 7

COVID-19 Global Data & Vaccination Progress Analysis

Python · Pandas · Seaborn · Matplotlib

Independent Data Analysis Project — Jupyter Notebook

Combined two large public datasets — global COVID-19 case/death data (from Our World in Data, in collaboration with the University of Oxford) and global vaccination data (from Our World in Data), both accessed via Kaggle — into a single merged dataset, then explored relationships between case rates, mortality, vaccination progress and socioeconomic indicators such as GDP and population density.

Data Merging Time-Series Analysis Correlation Analysis 12+ Chart Types
  • Merged two datasets (166,326 rows × 67 columns, and an 86,512-row, 15-column vaccination dataset) into a single 81-column, 172,134-row analytical dataset using a Pandas outer join keyed on date and country, then handled the resulting gaps with fillna and exported the combined frame to CSV for reuse.
  • Engineered features and standardised dates: parsed inconsistent date strings from both sources into a common format with pd.to_datetime, and derived new columns such as active cases (total_cases − total_deaths) to support later analysis.
  • Explored correlations between new cases, new deaths, total cases and total deaths via a correlation heatmap, and examined mortality against GDP category, population density and government stringency index.
  • Sliced the data per question using groupby, filter, isin and quantile calculations — for example, computing the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of total cases by continent and comparing new cases against new deaths for a chosen set of countries — so each chart was driven by a purpose-built subset.
  • Tracked trends over time — monthly case trends, yearly vaccination totals, and country-level active case trends (e.g. Australia).
  • Produced 15+ distinct visualisations — bar, scatter, pie, box, area, pair plot, heatmap, histogram, line, violin, strip and swarm plots — to communicate findings for different audiences and questions.
